title: The Hash Ring
description: A visual walkthrough of the consistent hashing ring — clockwise data placement, adding and removing nodes, and why only minimal data moves.

segments.text: Last lesson, we felt the pain of the rehashing problem. Today, we're going to see the elegant solution. Let me introduce you to the hash ring — one of the most beautiful data structures in distributed systems.

Imagine the entire hash space as a circle. The hash function outputs values from zero to some maximum, and we bend that number line into a ring. Zero meets the maximum at the top. Every possible hash value lives somewhere on this ring.
Now we hash each server's name or IP address, and place it on the ring at that position. Server A lands here, server B over there, server C down here. Each server occupies a single point on the ring.

To store a data item, hash its key and find that position on the ring. Then walk clockwise until you hit the first server. That server owns this data item. It's that simple — hash the key, walk clockwise, find the owner.

Let's place several keys. Key alpha hashes here, walks clockwise to server B. Key beta lands here, owned by server C. Key gamma goes to server A. Each server is responsible for the arc of the ring behind it, going counter-clockwise to the previous server.

Now watch what happens when we add a new server D. It gets hashed onto the ring between, say, server A and server B. Only the keys in that small arc between A and D need to move. Everything else stays put.
segments.thought_prompt: Compare this to modulo hashing — what fraction of data moves here versus the 75% we saw before?

segments.text: With N servers, adding one new server moves only about one Nth of the total data. That's roughly 25 percent with four servers, compared to 75 percent with modulo hashing. And this ratio gets better as you add more servers.

Removing a server is equally graceful. When server B leaves, its keys simply walk clockwise to the next server, server C. Only server B's keys are affected. The rest of the ring is completely undisturbed.

This is exactly how Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, and Akamai's CDN distribute data. The hash ring lets them add and remove nodes continuously without massive data reshuffling. It's production-proven at enormous scale.

But there's a catch. With just three or four servers, the arcs on the ring can be wildly uneven. One server might own 60 percent of the ring while another owns just 10 percent. The distribution is not guaranteed to be fair.
segments.thought_prompt: How could you make the distribution more even without adding real servers?

segments.text: That uneven distribution problem is exactly what we'll solve in the next lesson with virtual nodes. But for now, internalize this: the hash ring turns a catastrophic O of N data movement into an elegant O of one-over-N movement. That's the power of consistent hashing.
